blocks.text: It sounds too simple, but it's one of the most common calls. Make sure the thermostat is set to Heat, the temperature is set a few degrees above the room temperature, and no schedule or vacation mode is overriding it. If it runs on batteries and the screen is blank or dim, replace them.

blocks.text: 2. The air filter is clogged

runs.text: 2. The air filter is clogged

blocks.text: A dirty filter chokes the airflow. Many furnaces will shut the burners off to protect themselves from overheating, so you get weak or no heat. Turn the furnace off, slide the filter out and hold it up to a light. If you can't see light through it, replace it with the same size, arrow pointing toward the furnace. In winter, check it every month.

blocks.text: 4. The power is off

runs.text: 4. The power is off

blocks.text: A gas or oil furnace still needs electricity to run. Look for a switch near the furnace that looks like a regular light switch. It's easy for someone to flip it off by mistake, and if that's what happened, turn it back on. Then check your electrical panel. If the furnace breaker has tripped, you can reset it once. If it trips again, leave it off and call a technician, because something is causing it.

blocks.text: 5. The vent pipes outside are blocked by snow or ice

runs.text: 5. The vent pipes outside are blocked by snow or ice

blocks.text: High-efficiency furnaces vent through two white plastic pipes that usually come out the side of the house. After a storm, snow, ice or even a bird's nest can block them, and the furnace shuts itself off as a safety measure. Go outside and gently clear any snow around the pipe openings by hand. Don't stick anything inside the pipes. This one is very common across Long Island, New Jersey and Connecticut after a heavy snowfall.

If there's a blinking light on the control board, note the pattern for the technician.

blocks.text: If the burners come on but little or no air comes out of the vents, the blower motor may have failed. If the blower runs but the air is cold, a high-limit switch may have shut the burners off because the furnace overheated, often because of a clogged filter or blocked return vent. A loud hum, grinding or squealing is another sign the blower needs attention. On high-efficiency furnaces, a clogged condensate drain can also shut the system down. All of these need a technician to find the real cause, not just reset the switch.
